claims.text: 'Waived' is a statutory term of art traceable to a single sentence: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) substitutes, for the ordinary committee report, delivery of the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Nothing in section 119 requires that this delivery be written, recorded, retained, or shared with other members.

The parallel non-DoD, non-IC statute 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) contains the same waiver test ('would adversely affect the national security', 'case-by-case basis') but a materially WEAKER carve-down: 3348(e)(2) still requires the information to go 'to the congressional oversight committees', not merely to chairs and ranking members. The eight-member floor is therefore unique to the DoD statute.

The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.

claims.text: VERDICT ON THE BOARD'S QUESTION: the waiver has been exercised, and the Department of Defense says so in a currently effective, publicly released instruction - but no public document identifies a single specific instance, a count, a date, a program, or any connection to unidentified anomalous phenomena. DoD Instruction 5205.11, effective 12 September 2024, paragraph 1.2.f, states verbatim: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' This is not a hypothetical authority described in the abstract; the rest of the instruction is written around an existing population of such programs.

claims.text: THE STRONGEST SINGLE PIECE OF EVIDENCE THAT THE POPULATION IS NON-EMPTY IS A RECURRING REVIEW REQUIREMENT. DoDI 5205.11 requires that in its annual review the Special Access Program Oversight Committee - chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense - shall assess, among four listed items, '(d) All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' A standing annual agenda item to decide whether waived programs should REMAIN waived is only drafted if waived programs exist. This is a 2024 document, so the finding is current, not historical.

claims.text: The Department's own definition, from the DoDI 5205.11 glossary, verbatim: 'waived SAP - A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs.' And, adjacent to it: 'unacknowledged SAP - A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' A waived SAP is therefore a proper subset of the unacknowledged SAPs, distinguished precisely by the exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver.

The full public text of the 2024 directive - purpose, applicability, policy, all thirteen responsibility assignments, the governance section, the complete glossary and the reference list - contains no occurrence of the words 'waived' or 'unacknowledged' at all. claims.text: HISTORICAL CORROBORATION FROM A CONGRESSIONALLY CHARTERED COMMISSION. The Report of the Commission on Protecting and Reducing Government Secrecy (1997), Chapter II, states verbatim: 'Among black programs, further distinction is made for "waived" programs, considered to be so sensitive that they are exempt from standard reporting requirements to the Congress. The chairperson, ranking member, and, on occasion, other members and staff of relevant Congressional committees are notified only orally of the existence of these programs.' The same passage gives the surrounding population: 'There are approximately 150 DoD-approved SAPs (the exact number is classified and others have been created but not yet formally approved), down from 200 in the late 1980s, and roughly 300 SCI compartments, compared with an estimated 800 in the late 1980s.' The Commission gives no number for the waived subset. The phrase 'notified only orally' is the operationally important one: it describes a practice under which the 119(e)(2) delivery leaves no paper.

claims.text: GAO HAS DESCRIBED THE WAIVER MECHANISM BUT HAS NEVER PUBLICLY REPORTED AN INSTANCE OF ITS USE. GAO/NSIAD-93-78, the unclassified summary of a classified report, describes the mechanism verbatim: 'Section 119, 10 U.S. Code, enacted in 1987, requires DOD to submit annual reports to the congressional defense committees on special access programs. Under the law, the Secretary of Defense may waive the requirement that certain information on special access programs be included in the annual report if he determines that the inclusion would adversely affect national security. However, he must provide the excluded information to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' The report then never returns to the subject. Its findings on waivers are about a different thing entirely - 'DOD used waivers and exemptions to limit review, documentation, and reporting requirements' refers to Defense Acquisition Board reviews, competition requirements and Selected Acquisition Reports, not to Section 119(e). Do not let these two senses of 'waiver' be conflated on the board.

claims.text: WHAT SHOULD EXIST IF THE WAIVER WERE BEING USED, AND WHY NONE OF IT IS PUBLIC. Four artefacts are implied by the statute and the DoD instruction: (i) the underlying 119(a), (b) or (c) report itself, which is classified and, for (a) and (b), no longer statutorily required after 31 December 2021; (ii) the Secretary's case-by-case determination that inclusion would adversely affect national security, which 119(e)(1) requires to be made but does not require to be recorded in any publicly indexed form; (iii) the withheld information plus a written justification delivered jointly to twelve named members, which by the Moynihan Commission's account has historically been delivered orally; and (iv) the SAPOC annual review record of whether each waived program should retain that status, which is internal to the Department. None of the four is a public document class. There is no statutory requirement anywhere in Section 119 to report the NUMBER of waivers exercised, the fact that any waiver was exercised, or an aggregate count, to anyone outside those twelve seats. The absence of a public instance is therefore fully explained by the design of the mechanism and is NOT evidence of concealment beyond what the statute itself authorises.

claims.text: NO UAP-SPECIFIC EXERCISE OF THE 119(e)(1) WAIVER WAS FOUND IN ANY PUBLIC DOCUMENT. Searches across GAO's special access program series, DoD Inspector General audits and evaluations, Congressional Research Service products, and the Senate and House Armed Services Committee document sets returned no document in which a waived special access program is linked to unidentified anomalous phenomena, and no document in which any specific exercise of the Section 119(e)(1) waiver - UAP or otherwise - is identified, dated, counted or described. The DoD Inspector General's public catalogue for special access programs consists of external peer reviews and quality control reviews of the service audit agencies' SAP audit work, plus a series of entries titled only 'CLASSIFIED REPORT (Classified)'; none addresses congressional reporting under Section 119.
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually. Provides recommendations to the SAPOC concerning continued waived status.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 provides that the SRG 'Ensures the accuracy of the SAP list submitted to Congress prior to submission of the SAP annual report.'
DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 2 requires DoD SAPCO to establish 'the criteria for annual reviews of waived DoD SAPs by the SSWG and SRG.'

DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f limits access to waived SAPs, absent SecDef or DepSecDef approval, to 'the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees'.

A complete list of waived DoD SAPs demonstrably exists in documentary form, is reviewed at least annually by the Senior Review Group, and is validated by the SAPOC - which means the answer to 'how many waived programs are there' is a retrievable agency record and not an unknowable. Reasoning: DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3 assigns the annual review of all waived SAPs and the accuracy of the congressional SAP list to a named standing body.

desc: Stack the three documented mechanisms and the result is a program with the following properties, every one of which is sourced to a statute or a DoD issuance rather than to any allegation. Its existence is not acknowledged, affirmed or made known to any person not authorised (DoDI 5205.11 glossary). Its reporting to the defense committees under 10 U.S.C. 119(a), (b) and (c) has been waived by the Secretary of Defense on a case-by-case national-security determination, with the information going instead 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' (10 U.S.C. 119(e)). Within those committees, DoD policy limits access further: members generally 'shall be authorized access to DoD SAPs ... except for waived programs', and for waived programs 'only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors' unless the Secretary or Deputy Secretary approves otherwise (DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.f). Whatever paper the committee is shown stays in the building: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody' (para 4.h). If the program is executed at a contractor facility, a carve-out approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary removes DCSA inspection, DCSA information-system accreditation and the DCSA counterintelligence feed (32 CFR 117.6(b)(3); DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 2). Fraud, waste, abuse and corruption complaints must be reported 'through SAP channels' and not through collateral channels (DoDM 5205.07-V1 Enclosure 4). The Senior Review Group 'Reviews all waived DoD SAPs annually' and recommends to the SAPOC on continued waived status (DoDI 5205.11 Enclosure 3), so a record of every waived program exists and is reviewed once a year by a body chaired at Principal Deputy Under Secretary level. Nothing in this paragraph is contested. The contested question is only what is inside one of them.

claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) provides: "The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis."

10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) provides that when the waiver authority is exercised, the Secretary shall provide the withheld information and the justification for the waiver "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees" — and 119(g) defines the defense committees as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees plus the defense appropriations subcommittees of both chambers, i.e. six bodies and twelve members.

10 U.S.C. 119(b)(2)(B) requires each new-SAP report to include "an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice" — a comparative-technology disclosure that a 119(e) waiver can remove.
10 U.S.C. 119(f) prohibits initiating a special access program until the defense committees are notified and 30 days elapse after notification.

The annual reporting requirements of 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) terminated effective December 31, 2021, pursuant to section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, as recorded in the Termination of Reporting Requirements note to section 119.

DoD Instruction 5205.11, September 12, 2024, paragraph 1.2.f states: "The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight."

DoDI 5205.11 defines a waived SAP as "A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs."

DoDI 5205.11 defines an unacknowledged SAP as "A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(3) states: "Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense."

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.a(2) provides that access to a SAP umbrella conveys access to all subordinate compartments and sub-compartments "with the exception of waived sub-compartments" — meaning a waived sub-compartment can sit inside a program a member has otherwise been read into.

DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 7.2.c(1) limits committee professional staff access to non-waived SAPs only, and paragraph 7.2.f states flatly: "The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs."

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) is the statutory Gang of Eight provision: where the President determines it essential to limit access to a covert action finding, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking minority members of the intelligence committees, the Speaker and minority leader of the House, and the majority and minority leaders of the Senate.

50 U.S.C. 3093(e) defines covert action as activity "to influence political, economic, or military conditions abroad" and expressly excludes "traditional counterintelligence activities, traditional activities to improve or maintain the operational security of United States Government programs, or administrative activities" and "traditional diplomatic or military activities or routine support to such activities" — so a domestic material recovery, custody and exploitation effort would generate no Presidential finding and no reporting obligation under section 3093 at all.

50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(5)(B) requires that not later than 180 days after a limited-access statement of reasons is submitted, the President either give all members of the intelligence committees access to the finding or submit a renewed statement of reasons for continued limitation — a sunset discipline that has no counterpart in 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

connections: DoD SAPCO administers waived SAPs, controls congressional access requests, and can delegate Access Approval Authority for waived SAPs to its Deputy Director.
The SAPOC, chaired by the Deputy Secretary of Defense, is required by DoDI 5205.11 to assess in its annual review 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.'

FY2024 NDAA sec. 1687 (P.L. 118-31) attacks this mechanism directly by cutting funds for UAP activities 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations' unless details are given to the defense and intelligence committees and the four congressional leaders.

Senator Schumer's December 13, 2023 floor statement that information on UAP has been withheld from Congress 'especially as it relates to the four congressional leaders, Defense Committees, and the Intelligence Committee' is a direct reference to this reporting architecture.

David Grusch's allegation of programs concealed from congressional oversight is, in statutory terms, an allegation about either a waived SAP whose twelve recipients were not told the truth, or an effort operating outside the SAP system entirely.
10 U.S.C. 119 was added by Pub. L. 100-180 sec. 1132(a)(1), December 4, 1987 — the SAP reporting regime postdates by decades any program alleged to have begun in the 1940s or 1950s.
dossier.denialPosture: The Department's only public position on this mechanism is the single sentence in DoDI 5205.11 paragraph 1.2.f: "Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight." That assertion is true in the sense that twelve members are notified and false in the sense that ordinary committee process, staff review, and institutional memory are excluded by regulation in the same document.
dossier.narrative:
Read 10 U.S.C. 119 in order and the architecture assembles itself. Subsection (a) requires the Secretary of Defense to submit an annual report by March 1 on special access programs, including for each SAP a brief description, major milestones, actual cost by fiscal year, and estimated total and out-year costs. Subsection (b) requires a separate report by February 1 covering each new SAP — notice of the designation and the justification for it, plus the current total program cost estimate and, notably, "an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice." Subsection (c) requires 14 days' advance notice of any classification change or planned declassification. Subsection (f) forbids initiating a SAP until the defense committees are notified and thirty days elapse. Subsection (g) defines "defense committees" as the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees, and the defense appropriations subcommittees, of both chambers — six bodies.

Then subsection (e) removes it. "The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis." And paragraph (2): if the Secretary exercises that authority, the information and the justification go "jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees." Four committees, two members each. Eight.

The Department's implementing regulations are more specific than the statute. DoD Instruction 5205.11, reissued 12 September 2024, states at paragraph 1.2.f: "The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight." That last sentence is the denial, and it is doing a great deal of work. The glossary of the same instruction defines a waived SAP as "A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls than other unacknowledged SAPs" — and an unacknowledged SAP as "A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information."

Section 7 of DoDI 5205.11 governs congressional access and is where the twelve-member construct becomes operational. Paragraph 7.2.a(3): "Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs within their committee's respective oversight jurisdiction. Requests to access additional members of Congress or professional staff must be approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense." Paragraph 7.2.a(2) closes a gap that would otherwise leak: when a member is granted access to a SAP umbrella, that access carries down to all compartments and sub-compartments "with the exception of waived sub-compartments." Paragraph 7.2.b confirms that committee members get access to all DoD SAPs in their jurisdiction "except for waived programs." Paragraph 7.2.c(1) allows one majority and one minority professional staff member per committee access only to non-waived SAPs. Paragraph 7.2.f: "The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs."

So the practical picture: a waived unacknowledged SAP is briefed to twelve members plus staff directors and a security manager. Those members cannot discuss it with their own staff, cannot discuss it with colleagues, and cannot describe it publicly. The oversight that exists is the personal, unstaffed attention of eight busy legislators who cannot take notes out of the room.

Two further features deserve an analyst's attention. First, the sunset. The note to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that for termination, effective December 31, 2021, of the provisions in subsections (a) and (b) requiring submittal of an annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328. The reports the waiver was designed to redact stopped being statutorily required at the end of 2021. Whatever reporting occurs now occurs as a matter of practice, not obligation.

Second, the covert-action escape hatch. The Gang of Eight construct familiar from intelligence law lives at 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2): when the President determines it essential to limit access to a covert action finding, the finding may be reported to the chairmen and ranking members of the intelligence committees plus the four congressional leaders. But 50 U.S.C. 3093(e) defines "covert action" as an activity to influence political, economic or military conditions abroad, and expressly excludes "traditional counterintelligence activities, traditional activities to improve or maintain the operational security of United States Government programs, or administrative activities," as well as "traditional diplomatic or military activities or routine support to such activities." A domestic recovery, custody and exploitation effort — material retrieval on U.S. soil, laboratory analysis, contractor engineering — is not an activity to influence conditions abroad. It is therefore not a covert action, it generates no Presidential finding, it triggers no reporting under 3093 at all, and the twelve-member intelligence-committee mechanism never engages. The only mechanism that engages is 10 U.S.C. 119 — and 119(e) waives it.

That is the argument in its full form. Nothing in it requires anyone to have broken a law.

dossier.whatItIs: The waived unacknowledged special access program is the most restrictive reporting category in the American national-security system. It is created when the Secretary of Defense, acting under 10 U.S.C. 119(e), waives the statutory requirement that specified information about a special access program appear in the reports to Congress, and instead provides that information and the justification for the waiver jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the six defense committees. That is twelve members of Congress.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the mechanism that makes the board's premise legally possible without anyone committing a crime. A waived unacknowledged SAP is a program whose existence is affirmatively not acknowledged to anyone not cleared for it, whose contents are reported to twelve members rather than six bodies, whose professional staff are excluded by regulation, and whose contractor personnel are barred by DoD directive from taking material to any member of Congress without the approval of the DoD SAPCO director. Compounding this, the annual reporting requirements in 10 U.S.C. 119(a) and (b) — the very reports the waiver operates on — terminated by operation of law on December 31, 2021 under section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, so the statutory baseline against which a waiver would be visible no longer runs. If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort exists and has been kept from Congress, this is the container it fits in, and the container was designed and is administered lawfully.
